To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(1) NHC proteins are present at specific chromomeres in a reproducible and unique pattern, and (2) a major acidic NHC component is present at all chromomeres in an apparently uniform distribution.

the immunofluorescence patterns of the antisera against three different NHC proteins are unique, that the patterns of one antiserum are similar to the patterns obtained with antisera against molecular weight sub-fractions of NHC protein, and that one antiserum causes a general staining pattern.

the immunofluorescence patterns of individual NHC proteins on chromosomes are reproducible, unique, and selective; that at least some of the proteins are distributed in a pattern that mimicks DNA distribution; that some NHC proteins are present in a limited subset of chromomeric regions; that NHC protein distribution patterns may be used as genetic markers for chromomeric regions and for the identification of specific chromosomes; and that at least one of the major acidic NHC proteins is a general chromatin
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of individual proteins which play specific roles in maintaining chromatin organization.
the identification of individual NHC proteins and their characterization with regard to distribution patterns and molecular properties.
the identification of NHC proteins which play specific structural roles in the chromosome.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the NHC proteins are not distributed in a random pattern on the chromosome.
at least three NHC proteins are involved in the maintenance of chromatin structure.
the distribution of individual NHC proteins on the chromosome is variable, ranging from a very specific limited distribution pattern to a pattern that is very similar to that of DNA and histones.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
there are at least two distinct groups of NHC proteins.
NHC proteins are not randomly distributed in chromatin but are organized into specific subsets of chromomeres.
the distribution patterns of NHC proteins on polytene chromosomes are complex and varied, but the patterns obtained with individual antibodies are reproducible and unique.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the distribution patterns of the individual NHC proteins are highly selective and that the selective distribution patterns are reproducible.
the distribution pattern obtained with an antiserum against a specific NHC protein is not a general pattern, but rather is unique for that antiserum.

there is no single NHC protein that is distributed in a unique and reproducible pattern on polytene chromosomes, but that there are a number of proteins which appear to be present at specific sites on polytene chromo-somes in a limited number of reproducible patterns.
